classification.difficultyReason: Discover that evaluation at 1 bounds every coefficient, then choose an adaptive base so a second evaluation uniquely encodes the entire polynomial as digits.

content.prompt: Suppose a polynomial has non-negative integer coefficients. Is it possible to completely determine the equation of the polynomial, if you are only allowed to ask the value that it takes at two points?

answer.short:
Yes. Ask for $S=P(1)$, then for $P(N)$ where $N=S+2$.

The base-$N$ digits of $P(N)$ give the coefficients, from the constant term upwards.
answer.worked:
Write $P(x)=a_nx^n+\cdots+a_1x+a_0$, where every coefficient is a non-negative integer. First ask for
$$\begin{align*}S&=P(1)\\S&=a_n+\cdots+a_1+a_0.\end{align*}$$
Each coefficient is at most $S$. Choose the integer $N=S+2$, so $N\ge2$ and $0\le a_i<N$. Ask for the second value, $P(N)$:
$$P(N)=a_nN^n+\cdots+a_1N+a_0.$$
This is the base-$N$ representation of $P(N)$, with digits $a_n,\ldots,a_1,a_0$. Its unique digits determine every coefficient and hence the polynomial. If $S=0$, all coefficients are zero, so the polynomial is already determined.
